S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers shall report any thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a preliminary account of known facts and affected models. They shall provide affected customers with a safety notice within 48 hours, including known hazards, immediate precautions, and how to obtain assistance.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers shall report any thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a preliminary account of known facts and affected models. They shall provide affected customers with a safety notice within 48 hours, including known hazards, immediate precautions, and how to obtain assistance. A follow-up report with the investigation findings and corrective actions is due to the regulator within 30 days, or with an explanation and revised date if the investigation remains open. Reports shall include incidents regardless of whether the manufacturer considers the product defective.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C under a regulator-approved protocol. The maximum permitted failure rate is 5%. A model exceeding 5% shall submit a regulator-reviewed corrective-action plan and undergo verified retesting before new market placement resumes.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C under a regulator-approved protocol. The maximum permitted failure rate is 5%. A model exceeding 5% shall submit a regulator-reviewed corrective-action plan and undergo verified retesting before new market placement resumes. Manufacturers shall provide complete per-model test results to the relevant regulator and to customers purchasing that model before purchase. Individual-company per-model failure rates shall not be publicly disclosed.

parameters.quote: New units shall support remote emergency shut-off no later than 24 months after adoption, subject to regulator-approved cybersecurity and reliability requirements. Manufacturers shall retrofit already-installed units to support remote emergency shut-off within 6 years after adoption, where technically feasible, and report progress annually to the regulator.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: New units shall support remote emergency shut-off no later than 24 months after adoption, subject to regulator-approved cybersecurity and reliability requirements. Manufacturers shall retrofit already-installed units to support remote emergency shut-off within 6 years after adoption, where technically feasible, and report progress annually to the regulator.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New units shall support remote emergency shut-off no later than 24 months after adoption, subject to regulator-approved cybersecurity and reliability requirements. Manufacturers shall retrofit already-installed units to support remote emergency shut-off within 6 years after adoption, where technically feasible, and report progress annually to the regulator. If retrofit is not technically feasible, the manufacturer shall notify affected customers and provide an approved alternative emergency-safety measure.

parameters.quote: New units shall include built-in fire suppression no later than 36 months after adoption of this standard.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New units shall include built-in fire suppression no later than 36 months after adoption of this standard.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New units shall include built-in fire suppression no later than 36 months after adoption of this standard. Manufacturers shall document the suppression design and its validation under the regulator-approved safety protocol. This requirement does not waive incident-reporting, testing, or corrective-action obligations during the implementation period.

parameters.quote: A recall is mandatory when a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, or when the regulator determines that a serious imminent hazard warrants recall. Manufacturers shall promptly notify the regulator and affected customers when a recall is triggered and provide remedy instructions.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: A recall is mandatory when a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, or when the regulator determines that a serious imminent hazard warrants recall. Manufacturers shall promptly notify the regulator and affected customers when a recall is triggered and provide remedy instructions.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Manufacturers shall provide customers with model-specific safety notices describing material hazards, precautions, and assistance routes before purchase and promptly after any material new safety finding. A recall is mandatory when a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, or when the regulator determines that a serious imminent hazard warrants recall. The incident-rate trigger shall be assessed separately for each model, using incident counts and installed-unit denominators provided to regulators. Manufacturers shall promptly notify the regulator and affected customers when a recall is triggered and provide remedy instructions. Incident rates and recall notices shall be reported to regulators; individual-company per-model test failure rates shall not be publicly disclosed.

judge_section_notes: Final rules set strict S1 reporting (24h for all incidents, 48h customer notice), S2 5% test limit with sales stop until retesting, S3 24-month new-unit shut-off and 6-year retrofit, S4 36-month built-in suppression, S5 mandatory recall at 8/100k with prompt notices. All red lines are met: per-model results to customers but not public, retrofit ≥6 years, suppression ≥36 months. S3 new-unit deadline is 24 months, which is weaker than the acceptable 12 months.
